concepts.def: Random emission of radiation by unstable nuclei as they become more stable.
A helium nucleus (2p + 2n); highly ionising, stopped by paper or skin; range a few cm in air.
A fast electron from a neutron decaying to a proton; stopped by a few mm of aluminium.
High-frequency EM wave from a nucleus; very penetrating, stopped by thick lead or concrete.
Low-level radiation always present from rocks, cosmic rays, food, and medical sources.
Removal of electrons from atoms by radiation, which can damage cells and DNA.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Radioactivity & Particles — a core area of GCSE Physics.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Radioactivity & Particles brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Radioactivity & Particles.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Which radiation has the greatest penetrating power?
options: Alpha
Beta
Gamma
All equal
1 proton, 1 neutron
2 protons, 2 neutrons
1 electron
1 proton, 2 neutrons

mcqs.q: What absorber is needed to stop beta radiation?
options: Yes — only infrared and radio waves are non-ionising.
A sheet of paper — beta is only slightly more penetrating than alpha.
Thick lead — only lead can stop any radiation.
A few millimetres of aluminium (or similar thin metal sheet).

mcqs.q: Is radioactive decay periodic — does each nucleus decay at regular intervals?
options: Yes — half-life is the time between each emission from the source.
Thick lead — only lead can stop any radiation.
Yes — each nucleus 'ticks' at intervals of one half-life until it decays.
No — decay is a random process; half-life is a statistical property of a large population.
Yes — half-life is the time between each emission from the source.
No — its photon energy is below the threshold required to ionise atoms; ionising radiation includes UV (high energy), X-rays and gamma.
Yes — all electromagnetic radiation is ionising because it carries energy.
Yes — only infrared and radio waves are non-ionising.

options: Random emission of radiation by unstable nuclei as they become more stable.
Low-level radiation always present from rocks, cosmic rays, food, and medical sources.
High-frequency EM wave from a nucleus; very penetrating, stopped by thick lead or concrete.
Removal of electrons from atoms by radiation, which can damage cells and DNA.
